analysis.one_liner: Bars states from setting food safety warnings or rules stricter than federal standards.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 168 cosponsors and cleared committee 30–15, but never received a House floor vote before Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended federal food law to stop states and cities from keeping or creating food safety requirements and health warnings that differ from federal standards [S2][S3][S4]. Existing state rules would have had 180 days after enactment before being wiped out, unless the state petitioned the federal health department for an exemption or a national standard [S2][S3][S4]. States would have kept some narrow powers, including an 'imminent hazard' exception and laws on freshness dating, organic labels, and unit pricing [S3][S4]. The bill cleared the House Energy and Commerce Committee in October 2004 but never came to a floor vote before the Congress ended [S6].
analysis.who_benefits: Large food manufacturers and distributors, who would no longer have to meet a patchwork of state warning and safety rules and could label and sell products under one national standard. Retailers selling across state lines would also save compliance costs.

how_it_helps.text: States could not enforce any food requirement or safety warning not identical to federal law, ending state-by-state compliance burdens for food sold in interstate commerce [S2][S3][S4].
Existing state warning and safety rules would survive only 180 days unless the state won a federal exemption or a new national standard was created [S2][S3][S4].
States could petition for exemptions, but only if the rule protected an important public interest, did not conflict with federal law, and did not unduly burden interstate commerce [S3][S4].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers in states that had adopted stronger food warnings than the federal government — those warnings would be eliminated unless the state won an exemption. State health departments would lose their ability to act faster or tougher than federal regulators, and would bear the burden of petitioning to keep their own rules.

drawbacks.text: The bill would erase state food safety warnings and requirements that are tougher than federal rules, leaving consumers relying on whatever national standard the federal government sets, with states carrying the burden of justifying exceptions [S2][S3][S4].

Supporters' good-faith argument: a patchwork of 50 different state warning rules raises food costs and can confuse consumers, and the bill preserves exceptions for imminent health hazards and keeps laws on freshness dating, organic labels, unit pricing, and similar matters untouched [S3][S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Uniform national standards do reduce compliance costs for food companies, and some of that could reach consumers as lower prices. But the bill's core effect is subtractive: it removes state health warnings and safety rules without creating any replacement standard, and it shifts the burden onto states to petition and prove their rules are needed. The carve-outs (imminent hazard, dating and labeling laws) narrow but do not eliminate that loss. The trade runs mainly one way: industry saves compliance costs; the public gives up a layer of protection.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was reported out of committee and placed on the House calendar in October 2004, but the House never voted on it before the Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. Richard Burr (R-NC) introduced the bill on July 10, 2003, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, then to its Health Subcommittee [S6].
On September 30, 2004, the Energy and Commerce Committee ordered the bill reported (amended) by a vote of 30 to 15 [S6].
On October 8, 2004, the committee reported the amended bill with House Report 108-770 and it was placed on the Union Calendar (the list of bills awaiting floor action) [S4][S6].
The bill accumulated 168 cosponsors — 126 Republicans and 42 Democrats — but no floor vote ever occurred, and the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S5][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State governments and consumer and public-health groups that opposed the preemption kept the existing body of state food warning and safety laws, since nothing changed. Food manufacturers did not get the national uniformity they sought, though they could try again in a later Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: States and consumer advocates who opposed preemption

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship leaned heavily Republican (126 of 229 Republicans vs. 42 of 205 Democrats), and the committee vote was 30–15; the bill never reached the floor for a chamber-wide vote.

industries.note: The bill would have eliminated state safety requirements and warning laws not identical to federal rules, saving manufacturers the cost of complying with a patchwork of state standards [S2][S3][S4]. That saving comes directly from removing state warnings that inform shoppers about food hazards.
One national labeling and warning standard would simplify stocking and compliance across state lines. Retailers' gain mirrors the loss of state-level health warnings for their customers.

industries.industry: State food safety and consumer protection agencies
industries.note: States would have lost the power to enforce tougher or faster-acting food rules than federal law, except through a federal petition process or an imminent-hazard exception [S3][S4]. Their authority is the direct target of the bill.
